profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a B2B analytics software company that is preparing a six-week design-partner pilot for a new 'Lead-Lag Explorer' module based on robust detection of lead-lag relationships in lagged multi-factor models. The module has been proven in internal research on financial market data and in one environmental demonstration, and the team now wants to package it for two commercial prospects: an asset-management client and a sustainability advisory client. The agenda is to decide what materials will be included in the pilot package, what example use cases will be shown, what 'pilot-ready' means for the end-of-month milestone, who owns each workstream, and how the refresh process will be set up. The expected outcome is a seemingly aligned plan for deliverables, responsibilities, and timing for the pilot launch.

members.name: Maya Chen
members.expertise: Analytics productization, research-to-product transitions, quantitative workflow design
members.background: Maya previously worked in a quantitative research group before moving into product management at the company, where she translates experimental modeling methods into pilotable features for enterprise clients.
members.private_state: Maya wants to launch the pilot without creating new engineering dependencies, because her team has limited platform capacity this quarter and she needs the module to look commercially credible while still relying mostly on existing research assets and manual QA.
hidden_assumptions: A 'validation pack' is primarily an internal methods package that equips the account team with technical backup material, not something polished enough to send directly to clients.
The obvious 'environmental example' is the air-quality and temperature dataset used in the research materials, because it already has completed outputs and known caveats.

If something is described as 'pilot-ready', it means the model pipeline runs reliably on historical data and can be manually checked before each client meeting; self-serve delivery is not required yet.
When people say engineering can 'wire up the refresh', they usually mean operations can schedule an existing notebook against already-ingested data rather than build a new client-facing integration.
A client mentioning a data feed in sales discussions does not mean the feed is operationally available inside the product environment.

members.name: Daniel Ruiz
members.expertise: Enterprise pilots, solution packaging, pre-sales analytics storytelling
members.background: Daniel leads pilot design for strategic accounts and has spent the last eight years bridging analytics teams and commercial teams in fintech and data-platform businesses.
members.private_state: Daniel wants the pilot to feel client-facing and reusable across accounts, because he is under pressure to convert two late-stage prospects this quarter and needs materials that sales can send externally without a researcher in every meeting.
hidden_assumptions: A 'validation pack' is a client-ready appendix with interpretable charts, business framing, and compliance-safe formatting that can travel with a proposal or follow-up deck.
The natural 'environmental example' is the reservoir inflow and rainfall demo that the sustainability prospect already reacted positively to in an earlier sales session.
If a workstream is called 'pilot-ready', clients should be able to see refreshed outputs on at least a weekly cadence without needing a product manager to manually curate each run.
If account teams say the client's standard feed is 'already with us', that means engineering can treat ingestion as routine and include it in the pilot setup.
A pilot package should be designed as something that can be reused directly in live client conversations, not mainly as internal enablement material.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the validation pack
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that Maya will prepare the 'validation pack' for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya means a mostly internal methods bundle: model notes, caveats, sample outputs, and backup slides for the account team to use if technical questions arise.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel means a client-facing appendix: polished visuals, explanatory captions, proposal-safe language, and reusable charts that can be sent directly after the meeting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both organizations use the same phrase for adjacent artifacts, and each person hears a familiar deliverable name that normally does not require elaboration in a planning meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: Which environmental example they will show
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to including 'the environmental example' in the pilot materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya is thinking of the air-quality and temperature dataset from the research workflow, which already has robust cluster-level lead-lag outputs and documented assumptions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel is thinking of the reservoir inflow and rainfall demo from the sales repository, which was informally shown to the sustainability prospect and seemed commercially resonant.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both examples are legitimate internal references, both are known as the environmental example in different contexts, and neither participant expects that a non-finance illustration would need further naming.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the module should be 'pilot-ready by month-end.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya believes the milestone is met if the batch workflow reliably produces stable historical lead-lag summaries and she can manually QA outputs before client use.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel believes the milestone is met if clients can be shown refreshed outputs in a lightweight portal or dashboard on a weekly basis with minimal internal mediation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Pilot readiness sounds like a shared milestone rather than a contested definition, and both standards are common enough in enterprise software that each assumes the other is using the obvious one.

misalignment_points.topic: How the weekly refresh will be set up
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that 'engineering can wire up the refresh after handoff.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya expects a low-lift operational setup: schedule existing notebooks against already-available internal market data and manually add any supplementary outputs as needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel expects an engineering implementation that connects the client's standard feed, automates ingestion, and publishes refreshed results into the client-facing portal.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'wire up the refresh' hides major procedural assumptions, but in cross-functional planning meetings it often passes as routine implementation detail rather than something requiring explicit unpacking.
